failure_summary.description: A historical figure was answered with a full name for the wrong namesake ('Lucius Junius Brutus', fl. 510 BC). The clue's 44 B.C. detail fits Marcus Junius Brutus, and the answer key is the bare, commonly used name 'Brutus'.
The agent found the right work (the musical Show Boat) but the key spells it 'Showboat'. A spelling variant caused the exact-match miss, and it is not safely generalizable.

patch.reasoning: The Brutus miss is a systematic pattern: the agent used the headline entity of a passage (Lucius Junius Brutus) even though the clue's date and details fit a different namesake. It also gave a full name when the key uses the single name the person is universally known by. A short rule on one-name historical figures and namesake disambiguation covers this. The Show Boat miss is a one-off spelling variant, and a closed-compound rule would be speculative. Previous broad edits were rejected, so I am proposing one narrow edit.

edits.target: Never cut a part that identifies the person: keep the regnal numeral of a king or of a play's title character ('Richard III', not 'Richard'; 'Henry V').
edits.content: - Historical figures universally known by one name (ancient Romans and Greeks, other famous single-name figures): answer with that bare name as a trivia key would ('Brutus', 'Cassius', 'Cicero', 'Caesar'). Do not expand it to a full Roman name ('Marcus Junius Brutus') or to a namesake's name. When a passage is titled for one namesake (e.g. 'Lucius Junius Brutus, fl. 510 B.C.') but the sentence that matches the clue (a date such as '44 B.C.', an office, a deed) describes a different person, the clue's dates and deeds decide. The bare shared name is then the safest answer, and a different namesake's full name is wrong.
